column2: On the authority of Abū Ruqayyah Tamīm ibn Aws al-Dārī (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) that the Prophet (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said: “The religion is sincere counsel (naṣīḥah).” We said: “To whom?” He said: “To Allah, to His Book, to His Messenger, to the leaders of the Muslims and to their common people.” Reported by Muslim.
Al-dīn (“the religion”): the religion of Islam.
Al-naṣīḥah (“sincere counsel”): clearing oneself of any deceit towards the one counselled.
Qulnā (“we said”): we, the company of listeners.

“To Allah”: by believing in Him, denying that He has any partner, refraining from deviating with regard to His attributes, describing Him as He described Himself and as His Messenger described Him, and declaring Him free of all deficiencies;
desiring what He loves by obeying Him, fearing what angers Him by leaving disobedience to Him, and striving to bring the disobedient back to Him.
“To His Book”: by believing that it is His speech and revelation, reciting it as it deserves to be recited, revering it, acting on what is in it and calling to it.

“To His Messenger”: by affirming his message, believing in everything he brought, obeying him, reviving his Sunnah by learning and teaching it, following his example in his words and deeds, and loving him and those who follow him.

“To the leaders of the Muslims”: the rulers, by helping them in what they have been charged with, obeying them, uniting people around them, commanding them with the truth, and winning back to them hearts that have turned away;

conveying to them the needs of the Muslims, waging jihād with them, praying behind them, paying the zakāh to them, refraining from rising against them with the sword if they show injustice, and supplicating for their righteousness.
As for the leaders in knowledge, sincere counsel to them is spreading their knowledge, making their virtues known and thinking well of them.

“And to their common people”: by being compassionate towards them, guiding them to what is good for them, striving in what benefits them, keeping harm away from them, and loving for them what one loves for oneself and disliking for them what one dislikes for oneself.
The command to give sincere counsel.
It is called religion and Islam.
The term “religion” applies to action just as it applies to speech.

A scholar may leave the listener to work out the meaning of what he says, without adding further explanation until the listener asks; his soul will then be longing for it, so it makes a deeper impression on him than if he had been confronted with it all at once.
